nameStory: The 'Egyptian Walking Onion' has a wonderfully mysterious name! It's called 'walking' because it literally walks across your garden - the heavy clusters of baby bulbs at the top of the stalk eventually bend down and take root some distance from the parent plant. The 'Egyptian' part likely comes from Romani people who brought these fascinating onions to Europe from the Indian subcontinent, though they're not actually from Egypt at all!
description: Egyptian Walking Onion is a quirky perennial plant that looks like a regular onion gone wild. Instead of producing flowers like most plants, it grows clusters of marble-sized baby bulbs (bulblets) right at the top of its tall stalks. These bulblets can range from pea-sized to about an inch across and will actually start sprouting green shoots while still attached to the parent plant. It's essentially a self-propagating onion that can slowly 'walk' across your garden over the years.

idTips.label: Bulblets
idTips.description: Clusters of small, round bulbs growing at the top of tall stalks where you'd expect flowers - these marble-sized bulblets often have green shoots sprouting from them and smell strongly of onion when crushed

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, hollow, tubular green leaves that feel smooth and waxy to the touch - snap one and you'll get that unmistakable sharp onion smell and maybe even make your eyes water

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall stalks that start upright but often bend down under the weight of the bulblet clusters, creating an arching effect that helps the plant 'walk' to new locations

idTips.label: Underground Bulb
idTips.description: Tough-skinned, elongated underground bulbs that are quite pungent when cut - they can be leek-like and narrow or sometimes form bulbs up to 2 inches across

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Every part of the plant releases a strong, sharp onion smell when bruised or cut - often more intense than regular cooking onions

habitat: Egyptian Walking Onions are primarily found in cultivated gardens, herb plots, and sometimes escaped near old homesteads in New England. They prefer well-drained soil in sunny to partially shaded locations and are quite hardy, tolerating various soil types. You're most likely to encounter them in established perennial gardens where they've been growing and 'walking' for years.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge early and can be harvested as scallions - the fresh green shoots are tender and mildly onion-flavored, perfect for identifying the plant before bulblets form.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive bulblet clusters develop and mature at the tops of tall stalks - this is when the plant is most easily identified and when the 'walking' process begins as stalks bend under the weight.
seasonality.fall: Bulblets may take root if they've touched the ground, and the parent plant begins to go dormant - older bulblets that have rooted will show new green growth.
seasonality.winter: The plant dies back to its underground bulb, leaving little visible above ground except possibly some dried stalks - not easily identifiable during this dormant period.

funFact: This plant is essentially a time-traveler that can clone itself and migrate across your yard! A single Egyptian Walking Onion can theoretically 'walk' several feet per year by dropping its baby bulbs, which then grow up and produce their own walking offspring - meaning a plant you see today might be the great-great-grandchild of one that started yards away.
confusionNotes: Egyptian Walking Onions might be confused with regular chives or wild onions when young, but no other Allium species produces those telltale clusters of bulblets at the top of the stalk instead of flowers. Memory trick: if it's got baby onions growing where the flowers should be, it's a walking onion!
contextualKnowledge: Don't be confused by the many names for this plant - it's also called tree onion, topsetting onion, or spring onion depending on the region. Despite being called 'Egyptian,' it's likely a hybrid between shallots and Welsh onions and probably originated in Asia. The plant you find might be decades old, having slowly walked from an original garden planting.
compareHints: Unlike other New England Alliums such as wild garlic, chives, or wild leeks that produce typical flower clusters, Egyptian Walking Onion is unmistakable with its bulblet clusters. Wild garlic and field garlic have much thinner, grass-like leaves and produce small white or pink flowers, while wild leeks have broad, flat leaves that die back before flowering. The closest relatives in terms of use would be regular chives, but chives produce purple pom-pom flowers and stay in neat clumps rather than walking around.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wide leek stands out from other wild onions by having broad, flat leaves instead of narrow, tubular ones.
Wild garlic differs from other Alliums by its completely hollow, tubular leaves - wild leeks have flat, broad leaves, while chives have thin but solid leaves.
Unlike their larger cousins wild leek (ramps) which have broad, flat leaves, or wild garlic with its flat, grass-like foliage, chives have distinctively round, hollow leaves that are much thinner.

Among New England Alliums, garlic chives are unique for their flat, strap-like leaves - wild garlic has narrow tubular leaves, ramps have broad oval leaves, and regular chives have hollow cylindrical leaves.
Canadian Meadow Garlic differs from its cousin Wild Leek (ramps) by having thin, grass-like leaves rather than broad, flat leaves, and it grows in sunny areas rather than shaded forests.
Among New England's wild onions, nodding onion is the only one with distinctively drooping flower heads—wild garlic and field garlic hold their flowers upright in tight, rounded clusters.
Among its Allium relatives, garlic is distinguished by its segmented bulb structure — wild onions and leeks have single, solid bulbs rather than the characteristic cloves.
Yellow onion stands out from other New England Alliums by its bright golden-yellow flowers - most wild onions and garlics have white, pink, or purple blooms.
Common onions differ from their wild Allium relatives by having distinctly hollow, tubular leaves and that familiar sharp kitchen-onion scent.
Ramsons stands out from other New England wild onions by having the broadest, flattest leaves in the genus - most other Alliums here have narrow, grass-like or tubular leaves.

Wild leek stands out from other New England Alliums by being much larger and more robust - while wild garlic and chives have thin, grass-like leaves, and ramps have broad leaves that disappear before flowering, wild leek maintains its broad, blue-green leaves right through the blooming period.
Field garlic differs from wild garlic by having flower heads that contain both actual flowers and bulblets mixed together, while wild garlic usually produces only bulblets.
Unlike New England's native wild onions such as wild leek or wild garlic which have narrow, grass-like green leaves, Turkistan onion stands out with its broad, silvery-blue foliage.

Small Yellow Onion stands out dramatically from other New England Alliums due to its bright yellow flowers - most of our native and naturalized onions like Wild Garlic, Nodding Onion, and Wild Leek have white, pink, or purplish flowers.

Unlike other wild Alliums in New England like wild garlic or ramps, honey garlic has uniquely drooping, bell-shaped flowers rather than the upright, star-shaped or rounded flower clusters typical of most onion relatives.
